title: Animated pedagogical agents effects on enhancing student motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an animated pedagogical agent (APA) can improve students’ motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment. The authors focus on two motivational constructs from expectancy-value and ARCS frameworks: task relevance and self-efficacy. They also consider whether the agent’s gendered design matters, given prior evidence that girls often report lower science motivation than boys.

The intervention was an inquiry-based computer learning environment for kinematics called Motion, implemented in SimQuest. Students were assigned to one of three conditions: control (no agent image or voice), voice-only (audio messages from the agent without image), or embodied agent (image plus voice). The APA, Emma, was designed as a young, cool, female peer model and delivered motivational messages intended to support relevance and confidence. Participants were 61 third-year secondary school students in the Netherlands, approximately 14.7 years old, working individually on computers in a classroom setting.

Results showed that self-efficacy increased over time for all students, but task relevance did not change meaningfully. Girls rated the agent as a better model than boys, and there was a time-by-condition-by-gender interaction for self-efficacy during training: girls’ self-efficacy rose in the experimental conditions and fell in the control condition, while boys showed the opposite pattern. However, the APA did not produce significantly higher learning gains than the control condition; all groups improved on the knowledge test. The authors conclude that motivational scaffolding via pedagogical agents is promising but that effects are modest and depend heavily on agent design and the motivational needs of learners.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized experiment with a control group, multiple conditions, and repeated measures, which supports causal inference. However, it is a single small study (n=61) in one school, with some missing data and no independent replication in the paper.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear learning gains in the base inquiry environment and modest motivational effects for self-efficacy, but the agent did not improve learning outcomes over control. The impact is therefore informative but overall unclear/modest for educational implementation, especially for middle school math analog evidence.

interventions.use_case: computer-based inquiry learning environment in kinematics with embedded motivational animated pedagogical agent messages and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students in all three conditions made significant knowledge gains from pretest to posttest on a 27-item kinematics test, with no differences by condition or gender. The overall gain was large (total d=1.10, n=61), indicating the inquiry environment supported learning of the science content, but the animated pedagogical agent did not add measurable learning benefit over the control or voice-only versions.

Self-efficacy increased significantly over time for the full sample, with a large within-person gain from before to after training (d=0.51, n=61). However, condition effects were mixed: a significant time × condition × gender interaction emerged during training, with girls increasing self-efficacy in the agent and voice conditions while decreasing in control, but no main effect of condition on task relevance or overall self-efficacy.
finding.measure: Task relevance and self-efficacy ratings on a 10-point TRSE questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: Girls rated the animated pedagogical agent as a significantly better model than boys did. The difference was moderate-to-large (d=0.95, n=21 in the agent condition), suggesting the female embodied agent was more persuasive or relatable for girls than for boys.
finding.measure: Agent model appraisal questionnaire (11 items, 10-point Likert scale)
